why_how.text: Knowing who must hold a Nevada license, and how fast a newcomer must switch, keeps you driving legally from your first month here.
License terms change with age, so the expiry date on your card depends on how old you are when it is issued.

scenario.text: Dana moves to Reno from Oregon on the first of the month and keeps driving on her Oregon license.

reasoning.text: A new resident has thirty days after becoming a resident to apply for a Nevada license.

result.text: Dana must apply within thirty days, so by the end of her first month she should hold a Nevada license.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every Nevada license lasts eight years no matter the driver's age.

correction.text: A first license under sixty-five lasts eight years, but drivers sixty-five and older get four-year licenses.

memory_support.text: Under sixty-five, eight; sixty-five and up, four; ID cards, eight.

prompt.text: Sam is seventy and applying for his Nevada license. How many years will it last?

rationale.text: Licenses for drivers aged sixty-five and older are valid for four years, while younger first-time drivers get eight.

narration.text: This lesson opens the licensing chapter of the Nevada Driver's Handbook. Before any test, you need to know whether you need a Nevada license at all, how quickly a newcomer must get one, what the application asks for, and how long the card lasts. The answers depend on where you live and work, on your age, and on which card you choose. We will also look at the extra rule for applicants under eighteen, and at the one card that needs no Social Security Number. Keep an eye on the numbers, because the terms change with age.

lines.text: Live or work in Nevada and drive: you need one.
Border-state employees and stationed military are exceptions.
New residents apply within thirty days.

narration.text: Anyone who lives or works in Nevada and wants to drive on its streets and highways needs a Nevada license. The handbook names two exceptions: employees who come from neighboring border states, and military members stationed in Nevada. If you move here from another state, the clock starts when you become a resident. You then have thirty days to apply for your Nevada driver license. So a new resident cannot keep driving on an old out-of-state license for months; the switch is expected within that first month of living here.

lines.text: Fill out an application, visit a full-service office.
Be at least sixteen years old.
Prove name, age, residency and Social Security.

narration.text: Applying follows a set pattern. You fill out an application and visit a full-service DMV office. You must be at least sixteen years old. You then prove four things: your full legal name, your age, your Nevada residency, and your Social Security Number if one was ever issued to you. There is one notable difference for the Driver Authorization Card, often called the DAC: a Social Security Number is not needed to get it. A regular driver license applicant, by contrast, must prove the number whenever one has been issued.

lines.text: Under sixty-five: eight years, ends on your birthday.
No card ever lasts more than eight years.

narration.text: A first-time license issued to someone under sixty-five lasts eight years and expires on the holder's birthday. Drivers sixty-five and older get licenses valid for four years, while identification cards are valid for eight years. State law also sets a ceiling: a Nevada license or identification card can never be valid for longer than eight years. One special case applies when limited-term immigration documents were used to prove name and birth date. Then the license expires on the departure date verified by DHS, or after one year if DHS supplies no date.

lines.text: Four years at sixty-five and older.
ID cards stay at eight years.

narration.text: Here is a trap that catches many learners. Because the maximum validity is eight years, it is tempting to think every license lasts eight years. It does not. Unless limited-term immigration documents apply, the eight-year term is for a first license issued to someone under sixty-five. At sixty-five and older, the license term drops to four years. The identification card is different again: it keeps an eight-year term at any age. When a question gives you the driver's age, check it first, then pick the term. Mixing up the license term with the ID card term is the usual slip.

title.text: Check the term for a senior

lines.text: How long will his license last?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Sam is seventy years old and is applying for his Nevada driver license. How many years will that license be valid? Work through the age rule before you answer. Because Sam is sixty-five or older, his license is valid for four years. If Sam were forty without limited-term immigration documents, a first license would run eight years and end on his birthday. And if Sam only wanted an identification card, that card would be valid for eight years no matter his age. Age decides the license term, while the ID card term stays the same for everyone.

Let us sum up. Anyone who lives or works in Nevada and drives here needs a Nevada license, apart from border-state employees and stationed military members, and new residents apply within thirty days. Applicants must be at least sixteen and prove name, age, residency and any Social Security Number, though a DAC needs no Social Security Number. An applicant under eighteen needs a co-signer, such as a custodial parent or legal guardian, who shares liability for damage the minor causes by negligent or willful driving. Next we look at new residents and visitors.

why_how.text: New residents can skip some tests, but only when every transfer condition is met, so knowing the list saves a trip or a surprise.
Visitors and service members may drive on home-state licenses, and knowing their limits avoids an unlicensed-driving problem.

scenario.text: Luis moves to Las Vegas at twenty-five with a valid California license of the same class, two moving violations in four years, and no DUI.

reasoning.text: Every waiver condition must hold: fewer than three violations in four years, no DUI in seven years, a same-class license and age twenty-one or older.

result.text: Luis meets them all, so his knowledge and road tests can be waived, but he still takes the vision test.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing a clean transfer skips every test, including vision.

correction.text: The vision test is always given to a new resident; only the knowledge and road tests can be waived.

memory_support.text: Vision always; the rest only if all conditions fit.

prompt.text: Priya, twenty-three, moves here with a valid same-class license but had a DUI conviction five years ago. Can her road test be waived?

rationale.text: A waiver needs no DUI conviction within the past seven years, and five years ago falls inside that window.

narration.text: This lesson is about people arriving from somewhere else. A new resident transferring a license, an active-duty service member, and a student or tourist each face different rules. We will start with the rule that a Nevada resident may hold only one license or ID card, then see which tests a newcomer always takes and which can be waived. After that we look at the full list of waiver conditions, who may drive here on a home-state license, and how national databases follow a driver's record from state to state. Each rule is short, so learn them one at a time.

lines.text: Only one license or ID card.
The surrendered card is voided and returned.

narration.text: A Nevada resident may hold only one driver license or identification card. That means a card from another state, a US territory or a foreign country must be surrendered when you get your Nevada card. The surrendered card is voided and handed back to you, but it no longer works as a license. The goal is simple: one person, one active credential. Every driver record is also run through two national databases, the Problem Driver Pointer System and the CDL Information System, before a Nevada license is issued. One card, checked records.

lines.text: Fewer than three violations in four years.
Same class, valid license, twenty-one or older.

narration.text: A new resident always takes the vision test. The knowledge and road tests can be waived, but only when every listed condition is met. You must have fewer than three moving violations in the past four years, with no suspension, revocation or cancellation of your license. You must have no DUI conviction in the past seven years. You must have no restriction on your driving privilege that calls for an evaluation. You must hold a valid out-of-state license of the same class you are applying for, and you must be twenty-one or older.

lines.text: Two violations, no DUI, same class.

narration.text: Picture Luis, who moves to Las Vegas at twenty-five holding a valid California license of the same class. He has two moving violations in the past four years, no suspensions, no DUI, and no restriction calling for an evaluation. Go down the list. Two violations is fewer than three. No DUI within seven years. Same class, valid license, and he is over twenty-one. Every condition holds, so his knowledge and road tests can be waived. He still sits for the vision test, because a new resident always takes it, whatever the record shows.

lines.text: Waivers cover knowledge and road tests.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A spotless transfer does not mean no tests at all. The vision test is always given to a new resident. Only the knowledge and road tests can be waived, and only when all the conditions hold at the same time. Missing just one condition, such as a DUI conviction six years ago or being twenty years old, means no waiver. A second trap concerns other states: if your privilege is suspended, revoked, canceled or denied elsewhere, the national record check blocks a Nevada license until that issue is cleared, though an ID card may still be possible.

lines.text: Can her road test be waived?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Priya is twenty-three, has a valid license of the same class from her old state, and had a DUI conviction five years ago. Can her road test be waived? Think through the conditions before you answer. No, it cannot. One waiver condition is no DUI conviction within the past seven years, and five years ago falls inside that window. Because every condition must be met, failing this one means Priya takes the knowledge and road tests as well as the vision test, which a new resident always takes anyway.

lines.text: Active duty: home-state license is enough.
Visitors: sixteen, valid license, obey laws.

narration.text: To finish, think about drivers who do not need a Nevada license. An active-duty member of the US Armed Forces who holds a valid home-state license does not need a Nevada license. Non-residents such as out-of-state students, tourists and seasonal residents may also drive here without one, but they must be at least sixteen, hold a valid home-state license, and obey Nevada traffic and financial responsibility laws. So the service member has the simpler rule, while other visitors carry extra conditions. Next we look at the documents that prove who you are.

why_how.text: The DMV accepts only specific documents for name, birth date and Social Security Number, so bringing the wrong one means a second visit.
Some documents work only for certain cards, which matters if you want a Real ID.

scenario.text: Mei brings a hospital-issued birth certificate and a photocopy of her passport to prove her name and birth date.

reasoning.text: Hospital birth certificates do not count, and proof must be one unexpired original or certified document.

result.text: Neither item works, so Mei must bring an original such as a state-issued birth certificate or her valid passport.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming any birth certificate proves your name and age.

correction.text: A hospital-issued or foreign birth certificate is refused; a state-issued birth certificate or similar original document is needed.

memory_support.text: One original, unexpired, certified: no hospital copies.

prompt.text: Jordan wants a Real ID and can only bring a Nevada Department of Corrections ID card for name and birth date. Will it work?

answer.text: No, not for a Real ID.

rationale.text: A corrections ID card proves name and birth date for a standard card, but it cannot be used for a Real ID.

narration.text: This lesson covers the documents that prove who you are. The DMV needs proof of your full legal name and date of birth, proof of your Social Security Number, and in some cases proof of lawful status. Each kind of proof has an accepted list and a refused list, and some documents work only for a standard card, not for a Real ID. We will also look at name changes, immigration documents with limited terms, alternative documents that need approval, and the rules for translations. Knowing the lists before your visit saves you a second trip to the office.

lines.text: One unexpired original or certified document.
State birth certificate, passport or passport card.
Out-of-state Real ID with the approved mark.

narration.text: Proof of full legal name and date of birth is one unexpired original or certified document. Examples include a state-issued birth certificate, a valid US passport or passport card, a Consular Report of Birth Abroad, or another state's license, permit or ID that carries a DHS-approved Real ID mark. A Nevada Department of Corrections ID card can also prove name and birth date, but not for a Real ID. If your current name differs from your identity document, bring legal proof of the change, such as a marriage certificate, a divorce decree naming the change, an adoption record or a court order.

lines.text: Border Crossing and Consular ID cards.

narration.text: Several documents do not prove name and age. These include a hospital-issued birth certificate, a license or ID from another US state, territory or foreign country, a foreign birth certificate, a Border Crossing Card and a Consular Identification Card. An out-of-state Real ID marked limited term also does not prove name and birth date, so acceptable immigration documents must be shown instead. Compare that with the corrections ID card: it is accepted with a limit, for standard cards only, while the limited-term out-of-state Real ID is not accepted for either kind of card.

lines.text: Only the undated Resident Alien Card works.
Expired I-ninety-four needs an approved extension.
Limited-term documents give a Limited Term card.

narration.text: Immigration documents follow their own rules. An old Resident Alien Card printed with no expiration date is accepted as a Permanent Resident Card, but any other version is refused. The DMV will not make holders replace the undated card unless DHS asks, and the rules can change with DHS policy. An expired I-ninety-four, with a permanent-resident passport stamp or with a US visa, must be paired with a Notice of Action showing an approved extension. Limited-term documents, such as an Employment Authorization Card, produce a card marked Limited Term, and every immigration document is checked electronically.

lines.text: Card, W-two, form ten ninety-nine or paystub.
Originals showing the full number only.
Alternatives need approval, never Real ID.

narration.text: Proof of a Social Security Number can be a Social Security card, a W-two or IRS form ten ninety-nine showing the full number, or a paystub with your full legal name. Handwritten paystubs are refused, and every document must be an original that shows the complete number. If you cannot provide the usual documents, alternative documents for name, age and Social Security Number may be accepted with supervisory approval, but they can never be used to issue a Real ID card. Translated documents must cover the entire original, be typed or printed, and carry the translator's signed statement of accuracy and fluency.

lines.text: Real ID needs the full list.

narration.text: Here is a trap built on documents that work only sometimes. A Nevada Department of Corrections ID card proves name and birth date for a standard card, but not for a Real ID. Alternative documents approved by a supervisor also support a standard card, but never a Real ID. So if a question asks whether a document works, check which card the applicant wants. A second trap is the birth certificate itself: a state-issued certificate is accepted, but a hospital-issued one is not. The word birth certificate alone does not tell you the answer.

Here is a quick check: Jordan wants a Real ID and can only bring a Nevada Department of Corrections ID card to prove name and birth date. Will that card work? Decide before you read on. No, not for a Real ID. A Department of Corrections ID card can prove name and birth date for a standard card, but the handbook says it cannot be used for a Real ID. Jordan could use it for a standard card, or bring another accepted document, such as a state-issued birth certificate or a valid US passport, if a Real ID is the goal. Bring originals only.

Let us review. Name and birth date are proven with one unexpired original or certified document, and you bring legal proof if your name has changed. Hospital and foreign birth certificates, Border Crossing Cards and Consular Identification Cards are refused, as is a limited-term out-of-state Real ID. Only the undated Resident Alien Card is accepted, an expired I-ninety-four needs an approved extension notice, and limited-term documents produce a Limited Term card. Social Security proof must be an original showing the full number. Next, we compare Real ID with the standard card and the Driver Authorization Card.

why_how.text: Choosing between a Real ID and a standard card changes the documents you bring and what the card can do.
The Driver Authorization Card lets you drive but not identify yourself, so knowing its limits avoids problems later.

scenario.text: Ana holds a Driver Authorization Card and tries to use it as identification for a state benefit.

reasoning.text: A DAC is not valid for federal or state identification and cannot establish eligibility for Nevada benefits, licenses or services.

result.text: Ana cannot use the DAC this way, though she may keep using it to drive under the normal license rules.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a Driver Authorization Card as a form of identification.

correction.text: A DAC works like a license for driving, but it cannot serve as identification for any federal or state purpose.

memory_support.text: Gold star flies federal; DAC drives, never identifies.

prompt.text: Which mark tells you a Nevada card meets federal Real ID standards?

answer.text: A gold Nevada outline with a star cutout.

rationale.text: The Real ID card shows the gold outline and star and meets federal standards; a standard card says NOT FOR REAL ID PURPOSES.

narration.text: This lesson compares the three credentials in the licensing chapter: the Real ID compliant card, the standard card, and the Driver Authorization Card, known as the DAC. Nevada applicants may choose either a Real ID card or a standard card, and in either case the DMV must verify identity, birth date, Social Security Number, lawful status and primary residential address. The DAC has its own term, its own document lists and firm limits on what it can be used for. By the end you should be able to match a card to its markings, its documents and its uses.

lines.text: Real ID: gold Nevada outline with a star.
Standard: NOT FOR REAL ID PURPOSES.
Only Real ID meets federal standards.

narration.text: You can tell the cards apart at a glance. A Real ID license or ID shows a gold Nevada outline with a star cutout. A standard card carries the words NOT FOR REAL ID PURPOSES. The Real ID card meets federal standards, while the standard card does not. The Real ID Act of May two thousand five aims to fight terrorism, identity theft and other crimes by tightening the security of state-issued identification. That is why the evidence rules for Real ID are stricter than for a standard card, and why some documents only support the standard card.

lines.text: Two residency documents with your address.

narration.text: A Real ID applicant presents two documents proving Nevada residency that show the correct residential address, such as utility bills, mortgage statements, rental agreements or bank statements. If you already hold a standard Nevada license and want to upgrade to Real ID, you must again show documents for your name, birth date, Social Security Number and Nevada residential address, and they may be scanned, stored and electronically verified. Alternative identity documents can support a standard card with supervisory approval, but they are never accepted for a Real ID card, whatever the circumstances.

lines.text: Valid four years, ends on your birthday.
Renew and change address in person.

narration.text: A Driver Authorization Card is valid for four years and expires on the holder's birthday. The holder must carry it whenever driving, and renewals and address changes are done in person only. For a DAC you may show one document from the main identity list, or one of a US military ID, a military dependent ID, an Armed Forces discharge document or a Certificate of Degree of Indian Blood. Instead, you may show two documents from a second list, such as a foreign passport, a foreign birth certificate, a Mexican Federal Electoral Card or a Consular Identification Card.

lines.text: A DAC works like a license for driving.
It cannot prove eligibility for benefits.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A Driver Authorization Card works like a license for driving and follows the same rules unless the handbook says otherwise. Because it looks like a license, people assume it works as identification too. It does not. A DAC is not valid for federal or state identification, and it cannot establish eligibility for Nevada benefits, licenses or services. The handbook also says the information on a DAC application is not used to decide legal presence or immigration status. So remember the split: a DAC answers yes to driving and no to identification.

lines.text: Two Nevada cards side by side.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are looking at two Nevada cards. Which marking tells you that a card meets federal Real ID standards? Recall the two markings before reading on. The Real ID card shows a gold Nevada outline with a star cutout, and that is the card that meets federal standards. The standard card carries the words NOT FOR REAL ID PURPOSES and does not meet them. A Driver Authorization Card is a third case: it lets the holder drive, but it is not valid for federal or state identification at all. Markings settle the question quickly.

To wrap up, Nevada applicants choose between a Real ID card, marked with the gold outline and star, and a standard card marked NOT FOR REAL ID PURPOSES. Real ID applicants bring two residency documents, upgrades mean showing every document again, and alternative documents never qualify for Real ID. The Driver Authorization Card lasts four years, is renewed in person, accepts its own document lists, and works for driving only, never for identification or benefit eligibility. In the next lesson we look more closely at how every applicant proves a Nevada address.

why_how.text: Residency proof is required for original cards, and the wrong document can stall an application.
Young applicants often have no bills in their own name, so the handbook gives parents a way to prove the address for them.

scenario.text: Rob has lived in an RV park for twenty days and brings the park's record as one of his two residency documents.

reasoning.text: A hotel, motel, RV park or campground record counts only if it shows at least thirty consecutive days of living in Nevada.

result.text: Twenty days is not enough, so Rob needs a different listed document or must wait until the record shows thirty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming any stay record from a hotel or campground proves residency.

correction.text: The record counts only when it shows at least thirty consecutive days of living in Nevada.

memory_support.text: Two papers with your address; campgrounds need thirty days.

prompt.text: A sixteen-year-old applicant has no bills in her own name. How can her residence be proven?

answer.text: A parent or guardian proves it with two listed documents or signs a DMV-approved form.

rationale.text: For an applicant under eighteen, a parent or guardian can use two listed documents or sign a form confirming they share the address.

lines.text: Who must prove a Nevada address.

narration.text: This lesson is about proving where you live. Applicants for an original Real ID or standard ID card, an instruction permit or a driver license must prove a Nevada residential address, and Driver Authorization Card applicants must do so at original issuance. The handbook gives a list of acceptable documents, a special limit for temporary lodging records, a way for parents to prove a minor's address, and three department forms for unusual living situations. Getting this right is the difference between leaving with your card and coming back another day.

lines.text: One group dated recently, one last issued.

narration.text: Residency is proven with originals or certified copies of any two listed documents that show a Nevada residential address. The list is split into two groups: one group of documents must be dated within sixty days, while the other group may simply be the last one issued. Examples on the list include a notarized statement from the owner of the home saying the applicant physically lives there, and a voter registration card from a county clerk or registrar of voters. Whatever you pick, both documents must show your Nevada residential address.

lines.text: Lodging records need thirty consecutive days.
Parents can prove a minor's address.

narration.text: Some living situations have special rules. A hotel, motel, RV park or campground record counts as residency proof only if it shows at least thirty consecutive days of living in Nevada. For an applicant under eighteen, a parent or guardian can prove the applicant's residence with two listed documents, or by signing a DMV-approved form confirming they share the same address. The three department-approved residency forms are the Relief Agency or Shelter Certification, the Property Owner Residency Affidavit, and the Certification of Nevada Residency, each identified by its own DMV form number.

lines.text: A lodging record alone is not enough.
Thirty days in a row is the line.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A record from a hotel, motel, RV park or campground looks like proof of where you live, so people assume any stay record works. It counts only if it shows at least thirty consecutive days of living in Nevada. A guest who has stayed twenty days does not qualify yet. Consecutive matters too: separate short visits that add up to a month do not meet the rule. When a question gives you a lodging record, check for the thirty consecutive days before accepting it as one of the two residency documents. The rule is strict.

Here is a quick check: a sixteen-year-old applicant has no bills or statements in her own name. How can her residence be proven? Recall the rule for minors before reading on. A parent or guardian can prove the applicant's residence in one of two ways: by showing two listed residency documents, or by signing a DMV-approved form confirming that the parent and the applicant share the same address. Either path works, and the applicant does not need documents in her own name to meet the residency requirement for her first card.

lines.text: Lodging needs thirty days in a row.

narration.text: Let us review. Original Real ID and standard ID cards, permits and licenses all require proof of a Nevada residential address, and DAC applicants prove it at original issuance. You bring originals or certified copies of any two listed documents, following the dating rule for each group. Lodging records need thirty consecutive days, a parent can prove a minor's address with documents or a signed form, and three department forms cover shelters, property owners and other residency situations. The last lesson in this part covers the vision, knowledge and road tests.

why_how.text: Knowing what each test checks and costs helps you arrive prepared and avoid an automatic failure.

scenario.text: Kim answers a text message at a red light during her drive test.

reasoning.text: Using a cell phone during the drive test is an automatic failure.

result.text: Kim fails the test on the spot, no matter how well she drove before that moment.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a phone use during the road test only costs a few points.

correction.text: Using a cell phone during the drive test is an automatic failure, while other traffic-law violations are penalized.

memory_support.text: Phone in hand, test at an end.

prompt.text: Lee fails his knowledge test once and passes on the second try. What does that second attempt cost?

rationale.text: The initial tests cost twenty-five dollars, and each retest needed before the license is issued costs ten dollars.

narration.text: This lesson covers the tests you take to earn a Nevada license. There is a vision screening, a knowledge test, and a road test, each with its own rules. We will look at what happens if you need glasses, what the knowledge test checks and the ways you can take it, what the tests cost, how the examiner checks your vehicle before the road test, what the road test scores, and the one action that ends a drive test immediately. Knowing these rules in advance helps you arrive prepared and keeps a simple mistake from costing you the test.

lines.text: Glasses or contacts add a restriction.
Signs, markings, laws and safe practices.
Oral exam on request; Spanish offered.

narration.text: If you need glasses or contact lenses to meet the vision standard, a restriction is placed on your license. The knowledge test checks highway signs and markings, traffic laws and safe driving practices, and it is given on automated equipment or on paper. An oral exam can be requested, and Basic Class C testing is also offered in Spanish. The initial knowledge and skills tests carry a twenty-five dollar fee, and each retest needed before the license is issued costs ten dollars. So a failed attempt costs you time and a small extra fee.

lines.text: Lights, signals, horn, belts, tires, wipers.

narration.text: Before the road test, the examiner checks your registration and plates, your proof of insurance, and the headlights, taillights, brake lights, turn signals, horn, seat belts, tires and windshield wipers. The test vehicle must be safe, with working brakes, speedometer and muffler, and a clean, safe seat for the examiner. No passengers or animals may ride along. If the vehicle fails any of these checks, the drive cannot go ahead, so every light, signal and required part needs to be working when you arrive for the test.

lines.text: No parking assist or cruise control.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Most mistakes on the road test are scored, so learners assume every error just costs points. One does not. Using a cell phone during the drive test is an automatic failure, and aids such as parking assist and cruise control may not be used. Breaking a traffic law during the test is penalized as part of the scoring. So separate the two ideas: a traffic-law violation counts against you, while touching your phone ends the test outright. Put the phone away before you start the engine and leave it there.

lines.text: Lee needs a second knowledge test.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Lee fails his knowledge test on the first try and passes on the second, before his license is issued. What does that second attempt cost him? Recall the two fees before you answer. The second attempt costs ten dollars. The initial knowledge and skills tests carry a twenty-five dollar fee, and each retest needed before the license is issued costs ten dollars. So the first fee covers the first attempts, and every extra attempt adds the smaller retest fee until the license is finally issued to the applicant.

lines.text: You may stop on a grade.

narration.text: To close, the road test scores how you prepare, control the car, enter traffic, use lanes, control speed, turn, park, back up, stop, pass, and watch traffic, and you may be asked to stop on a grade. Breaking a traffic law during the test is penalized, and using a cell phone is an automatic failure. Remember the earlier pieces too: a restriction for glasses or contacts, a knowledge test on signs, laws and safe practices, and a vehicle that passes the examiner's checks with no passengers aboard. That completes the first part of the licensing chapter.
